planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in spring into permanently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in part shade; this stream-side species needs steady moisture at the root and resents drying out between waterings.

directions: Thunberg's helleborine is a cold-hardy terrestrial orchid from streamside meadows and wet woodland margins stretching from the Russian Far East to Japan and the Ryukyu Islands, closely related to the North American Epipactis gigantea but tougher in winter cold. In early to midsummer it sends up leafy stems bearing loose spikes of orange-yellow flowers marked with pink, and over a few seasons it spreads gently by rhizomes to form a modest colony. Give it a permanently damp, humus-rich spot such as a bog bed, pond margin, or rain garden in dappled shade, since it struggles wherever soil is allowed to dry out. It pairs naturally with other moisture-loving shade orchids and ferns in a woodland seep garden.

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in part shade; this is one of the more cold-tolerant deciduous Calanthe species, native to cool mountain forests of Japan.

directions: Nippon mountain calanthe is a deciduous terrestrial orchid native to cool, high-elevation coniferous and mixed woodlands of Japan and Xizang, where it grows from clustered pseudobulbs topped with broad, pleated leaves. In early to midsummer it sends up a loose spike of small, chartreuse-white flowers, more muted than the showier purple-and-white blooms of its lowland relative Calanthe discolor, but valued for its ability to tolerate colder winters. Plant divisions in humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in dappled shade and let it settle in undisturbed for a season or two before expecting flowers. It suits a cool, shaded corner of the woodland garden alongside other hardy Asian terrestrial orchids.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in part shade; this circumboreal species comes from cold northern forests and needs a hard winter chill, performing poorly and often only briefly in warm-summer gardens.

directions: Spotted lady's slipper is a diminutive circumboreal orchid found in cool forests and thickets across Belarus, Russia, Siberia, China, Korea, and Japan to Alaska and the Yukon, making it one of the most cold-adapted members of the genus. Each short stem carries a pair of clasping, pleated leaves below a single small pouch flower patterned in magenta and white, opening in late spring to early summer. It is notoriously short-lived in cultivation outside genuinely cold, boreal-type climates, so gardeners outside its comfort zone should treat any planting as an experiment rather than a guaranteed long-term colony. Give it humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded site that mimics its native forest floor, and never dig wild plants.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall into humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; this species is grown as much for its dramatic fan-shaped, pleated foliage as for its flower.

directions: Japanese fan-leaf lady's slipper is prized among hardy-orchid collectors for its striking foliage: a single pair of broad, deeply pleated, fan-shaped leaves held nearly horizontal, making it ornamental even before it blooms. In spring a solitary stem rises between the leaves to hold one pale pink-to-purple pouch flower with twisted side petals, native to woodland slopes of Japan, Korea, and central China. Plant rhizomes in humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade, and protect emerging shoots from late spring frost, since they appear early and are briefly tender. Once established it slowly forms multi-stemmed clumps, rewarding patient woodland gardeners with one of the most architecturally distinctive leaves in the genus.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; the dark green, non-golden foliage of this miniature cultivar tolerates considerably more shade than the gold-leaved pisifera cultivars without losing color.

directions: Tsukumo is a true miniature Sawara cypress selection from Japan that builds a dense, irregular, cushion-like mound of soft, dark green, juvenile-type foliage sprays rather than the flattened, thread-like or moss-like textures of its better-known pisifera relatives. Growth is extremely slow, so it holds its tight, rounded outline for years without pruning, making it a long-term centerpiece for a trough, rock garden, or miniature conifer collection. Because it keeps its deep green color without the intense sun exposure that gold-foliage pisifera forms need, it is a good choice for a lightly shaded dwarf-conifer bed. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, since Chamaecyparis pisifera resents both drought and waterlogging.

planting.note: Site in full sun in well-drained soil; this old, very low-growing juniper selection is useful for rock gardens, troughs, and the front of a dwarf conifer bed where a true ground-hugging form is wanted.

directions: Pygmy singleseed juniper is an old, slow-growing cultivar valued for its tight, low, mounding to semi-prostrate habit, clothed in dense, blue-green, scale-like foliage that stays fine-textured rather than coarsening with age. It spreads wider than it grows tall, creeping gradually over rocks or gentle slopes without ever becoming rangy, which has kept it in circulation in rock-garden and alpine-conifer collections for generations. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, since like most Juniperus squamata forms it dislikes heavy, wet ground and is prone to foliage dieback in poorly drained sites. Its diminutive scale makes it a natural companion for other true miniature and dwarf conifers in a trough or scree planting.

planting.note: Site in full sun in well-drained soil; this true miniature spruce, sourced as a witch's-broom sport from 'Skylands', adds only a fraction of an inch per year and is best appreciated up close in a trough or rock garden.

directions: Tom Thumb is a true miniature selection of Oriental spruce, forming a tight, slow-building nest-like mound of short, glossy, dark green needles densely set on congested branching. Its growth rate is exceptionally slow even by dwarf-conifer standards, so it remains a tidy, compact dome for many years and rarely needs pruning to keep its shape. This scale makes it a favorite for miniature conifer collections, trough gardens, and rock gardens, where larger spruce cultivars would quickly outgrow the space. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid sites with standing winter moisture, which can cause needle and root problems in dwarf spruce selections.

planting.note: Site in full sun in well-drained soil; like most dwarf Colorado blue spruce selections, it originated as a witch's-broom sport and keeps a congested, irregular habit rather than the symmetrical cone of the full-size species.

directions: Sester Dwarf is a slow-growing, irregularly globose to mounded dwarf form of Colorado blue spruce, carrying the same stiff, powder-blue needles as the full-size species in dense miniature proportions. Like several other named dwarf Picea pungens selections, it traces to a witch's-broom sport rather than a seedling, which gives it its congested, cloud-like branching rather than a symmetrical pyramidal shape. It makes a strong blue accent in a rock garden or dwarf-conifer bed without ever approaching the bulk of a standard blue spruce. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, since good color and tight growth both depend on strong light and soil that doesn't stay wet through winter.
